title: Samson's Wedding, Riddle and Revenge
overview: Samson insists on marrying a Philistine woman, and a wedding bet over a riddle turns into betrayal and bloodshed that begins his fight with the Philistines who ruled Israel.

parts.label: A disputed choice of wife (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: His parents object because Israelites were expected to marry within their own people, not the 'uncircumcised' Philistines who ruled over them. The writer says the LORD was using this to start a conflict, though readers debate whether God approved the choice or simply worked through Samson's stubborn desire.

parts.label: The lion and the honey (vv. 5-9)
parts.note: A sudden rush of strength from God's Spirit lets Samson kill a young lion with his bare hands, and later he scoops honey from its carcass. He had been set apart to God from birth under rules that included avoiding dead bodies, so many readers take his secret snack as a sign he treated that vow lightly.

parts.label: The wedding feast bet (vv. 10-14)
parts.note: At the week long feast, thirty local men are assigned as his companions, and Samson bets them thirty linen garments and thirty sets of clothes, a costly stake. His riddle points to the lion and the honey, something only he had seen, so it was nearly impossible to guess.

parts.label: Threats, tears and betrayal (vv. 15-18)
parts.note: The guests threaten to burn his bride and her family alive, so she pleads with him until he gives her the answer. His reply about plowing with his heifer is a farm image meaning they won only by using his wife against him.

parts.label: Killing at Ashkelon (vv. 19-20)
parts.note: To pay the bet, Samson goes to another Philistine city, kills thirty men and hands over their clothes. The text links this to the Spirit's power without praising it, and his bride is given to one of his companions, setting up the revenge of the next chapter.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether Samson should be read mainly as a hero of faith whom God empowered, or as a deeply flawed man whose selfish choices God used in spite of himself.
think: When someone does real harm while also, in some way, serving a larger cause, how do you weigh the two against each other?
